tip: For feelings and states, use 'estar com' plus a noun: 'tô com uma preguiça' is literally I'm with a laziness, meaning I feel so lazy.
Portuguese takes breakfast rather than has it: 'tomaram café da manhã' uses the same 'tomar' you use for drinks.
'Esquentar a cabeça' literally is to heat the head and means to worry. 'Não esquenta a cabeça' = don't stress about it.
'Pois é' is a common filler/agreement expression meaning 'yeah' or 'exactly' or 'that's how it is.' Used to show empathy or agreement.
'Oxe' is an exclamation from Northeastern Brazil expressing surprise or confusion. It's spread across the whole country.
'Tomara que' means I hope that, and the verb after it shifts form: 'dê', not 'dá'. You'll hear it so often you'll learn it as a set phrase.
'Tô ligado' literally means I'm switched on, and as slang it means I'm aware or I got it. 'Tô ligado' = understood.
'Dar certo' is one of the most important Brazilian expressions. It means 'to work out/to go well.' 'Vai dar tudo certo' = it'll all be fine.
'Pera aí' is a contraction of 'espera aí' (wait there). Very common in casual speech.
'Faz parte' means 'it's part of life' or 'it happens.' 'Vida que segue' = life goes on. Together, they form a very Brazilian philosophical acceptance.
'Gente' usually means people, but 'gente boa' describes one kind, decent person. 'Muito gente boa' = a really good person.
Adjectives usually follow the noun, so the card says 'emprego novo' rather than putting 'novo' first.
'Estar de saco cheio' is a mildly crude idiom for being fed up. 'Tô de saco cheio disso' = I'm sick of this.
'Rodízio' is a Brazilian dining style where servers bring endless rounds of meat (or pizza, sushi, etc.) to your table. Very popular.
'Que' (that) can't be dropped: 'notei que ele estava' = I noticed [that] he was. English can omit it.
'Trouxe' is the irregular past of 'trazer' (to bring), not a regular ending. 'Ele trouxe comida' = he brought food.
'Coitado/coitada' means 'poor thing.' Used to express sympathy. It's not rude – it's genuinely empathetic.
'Fazer uma pergunta' pairs 'fazer' (to make) with 'pergunta' to mean ask a question. 'Posso te fazer uma pergunta' = can I ask you a question.
'Estar de olho em' means to keep an eye on someone. 'Tô de olho em você' = I'm watching you, as a playful warning.
'Saber' past: 'ele soube'. The past of 'saber' often means 'found out' – a completed discovery.
'Almoçamos' is the same for present and past (the 'nós' form). Context tells you which tense: 'ontem almoçamos' = past, 'sempre almoçamos' = present.
'Dele' is 'de' + 'ele' and means his. 'O nome dele' = his name. Portuguese puts the owner after the noun.
With a finished action, 'há' before a time span means ago: 'há seis meses' = six months ago.
'Fazer questão de' means to insist on, literally to make a point of, so 'fez questão de pagar' means he insisted on paying.
'A gente' means we but takes a singular verb: 'a gente chegou', not 'chegamos'.
'A gente' means we in casual speech but takes a singular verb, like 'ele': 'a gente fez' = we did.
'Pode deixar' means 'leave it to me' or 'don't worry about it.' It's a very reassuring Brazilian expression.
'Ir' past: 'vocês foram'. 'Foram' is past of both 'ir' and 'ser' – context tells which. Here: 'went.'
'Dar uma olhada' means to take a quick look: 'dei uma olhada no cardápio' = I glanced at the menu.
'Mudar de ideia' = change your mind, and the 'de' is required: Portuguese changes of something, as in 'mudar de casa' (move house).
